source.title: Exploring Loss Landscapes through the Lens of Spin Glass Theory
source.authors: Hao Liao; Wei Zhang; Zhanyi Huang; Ze-Mei Long; Mingyang Zhou; Xiaoqun Wu; Rui Mao; C. Yeung

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper and supplementary material; some figure captions and appendix text have minor wording or formatting errors, but the relevant results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures how batch size, width and loss-landscape flatness relate to train and test performance in shallow ReLU networks, using interpolation and accuracy comparisons rather than the original studies' protocols.
record.gate_note: The paper reports that small-batch solutions are flatter and have higher test accuracy than large-batch solutions, along with explicit MNIST train/test accuracies by width and batch size. It also reports solution-distance distributions and random walks, but those do not directly measure the train/test gap and are not rows for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: Table A3 tests continued generalization with increasing width (V2) and held-out performance differences between batch sizes (V5). The epoch budget is unspecified, so the fixed-budget condition of V5 cannot be verified. The flatness experiment does not measure the magnitude-aware sharpness named by V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that flatter local minima correlate with improved generalization, supported by their small- versus large-batch MNIST experiments. They explicitly limit extrapolation to more complex architectures.
record.recipe_differences: Uses single-hidden-layer ReLU fully connected networks trained on MNIST, Adam, batch-size comparison and interpolation between solutions; the target versions describe broader benchmark and optimizer recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size changes the measured flatness and test accuracy; the authors state that small-batch minima become flatter as hidden-node count increases.

fits_no_version.finding: Small-batch solutions have flatter loss profiles along the line connecting small- and large-batch solutions and higher test accuracy; the small-batch profiles flatten further with width.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Directional interpolation flatness correlates with better held-out accuracy in these shallow MNIST networks. This does not test magnitude-aware sharpness in V7.

fits_no_version.finding: Adam and SGD produce different distributions of distances between trained solutions and different clustering structures.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer choice affects the geometry of trained solutions; these measurements do not establish an optimizer generalization advantage.

record.problems: The experiments focus on shallow fully connected networks, and the authors say this limits generalization to other architectures. Table A3 reports no uncertainty values, despite saying means and standard deviations were recorded. The main text gives no exact numerical flatness or test accuracy values for the interpolation comparison.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported qualifying results for V2 were extracted: the width-dependent test accuracies are presented in Table A3 only as a batch comparison, not as a direct width sweep against a stated interpolation threshold. Other plots on random walks, permutation interpolation and solution clustering measure loss-landscape structure but not the train/test generalization gap named by these versions.

untested.parts: No comparison between natural-label and fixed-random-label training.

The interpolation threshold is not located; training accuracy is rounded to 99.99%, rather than demonstrated zero error. Training to convergence and absence of explicit regularization are not documented sufficiently to verify the original recipe.
No convolutional versus fully connected held-out performance comparison.
Optimizer comparisons concern distances between solutions, not comparative held-out performance under specified tuning.
Equal epoch budgets are not established. No workload-dependent batch threshold, language-model experiment, or recipe adaptation is tested.
No magnitude-aware weight-perturbation measure, convolutional-family comparison, or ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
No removal of examples selected by memorization influence followed by retraining.

record.verdict_notes: The record incorrectly says exact batch sizes are unavailable: Section 4.5 specifies 256 and 10% of training samples, giving 6,000 for MNIST. Table A3 contains no numerical uncertainty estimates despite the five-run statement. Width comparisons are recoverable from existing rows and are already acknowledged in rows_left_out, so no missing-result entry is needed.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare fitting natural labels with fitting fixed random labels.
Tests wider MNIST networks after both batch-size treatments, but does not report a sweep identifying the width at which zero training error first occurs or test error at each width.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD held-out performance comparison.

Tests small versus large batch on MNIST with Adam, but does not provide the exact batch sizes, does not report language models, and does not test longer training, warmup, normalization or other recipe adaptations.

Tests whether flatter minima correspond to better generalization using interpolation between batch-size solutions; does not use magnitude-aware weight perturbations or compare the measure with norm- and margin-based measures.
No memorized-example removal or retraining experiment.
